summary: A 1977 list of assigned numbers used in network protocols, such as protocol and port assignments. It replaced RFC 503 and RFC 604 and was replaced by RFC 750. It is historic.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 739 is a catalog of number assignments for early network protocols, including link numbers, socket numbers, network numbers, and message identifiers. It says the catalog would be updated periodically; RFC 750 later obsoleted it.

questions: how were socket numbers grouped in rfc 739
what is the difference between link and socket numbers
subtitle: A 1977 catalog of assigned link, socket, network, and message numbers.

tldr.problem: Network protocols and services needed shared number assignments to identify links, sockets, networks, and message types.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 739 publishes assigned values and identifies the contact for obtaining new assignments.
tldr.outcome: RFC 739 is Historic, obsoleted RFC 503 and RFC 604, and was obsoleted by RFC 750.

today: RFC 739 is Historic and was obsoleted by RFC 750. It obsoletes RFC 503 and RFC 604.

sections.title: A Periodic List of Assignments
sections.content:
RFC 739 documents currently assigned values from several number series used in network protocol implementations. It says the RFC would be updated periodically and directs people developing protocols or applications that need assigned values to contact Jon Postel.

The memo includes tables for links, sockets, network numbers, Internet message versions, message formats, and message types.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo is a reference list of assigned values. Developers were directed to request numbers from the person responsible for the assignments.

sections.title: Links, Sockets, and Networks
sections.content:
The link field described in the memo is the high-order 8 bits of a 12-bit message identifier. The link table assigns ranges to AHHP control and regular messages, reserves ranges, and includes experimental protocols.

Socket numbers name endpoints of logical connections and are divided into four ranges: 0-63 for network-wide standard functions, 64-127 for host-specific functions, 128-223 reserved for future use, and 224-255 for experimental functions. The network-number field is 8 bits and the table assigns values to networks such as ARPANET and CYCLADES.
sections.plainLanguage: Links, sockets, and networks each have assigned number ranges. The tables identify which values are standard, host-specific, reserved, or experimental.

sections.title: Internet Message Identifiers
sections.content:
The RFC lists a 4-bit field for the Internet message version, with value 1 marked current in this edition. It also lists an 8-bit field for Internet message formats and a separate 4-bit field for message types.

These tables record the assignments as published in this historical edition.
sections.plainLanguage: Version, format, and type fields tell a receiver how to interpret a message. This RFC records the numbers assigned to those fields at the time.
